title: The tail that reacts
hook: Warm a reaction by 3%. Why can it run almost twice as fast?

knows: that molecules must collide hard enough to react (an energy barrier)
doesNotKnow: that collision energies are spread out, with a thin high-energy tail
why a small temperature rise can double a rate

misconception: Rate rises in proportion to how much hotter it gets: about 3% hotter, about 3% faster.
objective: The learner can explain that only the far tail of collision energies clears the barrier, and a small warming barely moves the crowd but nearly doubles that tail: with a 50 kJ/mol barrier, 298 K to 308 K gives about 1.9 times the rate.

claims.text: In simple collision theory the share of collisions with at least the barrier energy Ea is e^(−Ea/RT), and the rate is proportional to it (the Arrhenius form k = A e^(−Ea/RT)).
claims.source: Atkins & de Paula, Physical Chemistry, chapters on reaction rates (Arrhenius equation) and collision theory (fraction of collisions with energy along the line of centres >= Ea is exp(-Ea/RT)).
CODATA 2018: R = 8.314462618 J mol^-1 K^-1 (exact since the 2019 SI redefinition, as N_A x k).

claims.text: With Ea = 50 kJ/mol, warming from 298 K to 308 K multiplies the rate by about 1.9.
claims.source: ratio = exp[(Ea/R)(1/298 - 1/308)] = exp[6014 x 1.0895e-4] = exp(0.655) = 1.93 (node script). Assumes A unchanged.

claims.text: About 1.7 collisions per billion clear a 50 kJ/mol barrier at 298 K and about 3.3 per billion at 308 K.
Ea/RT is about 20 at 298 K, so a 3% change in T is about a 0.65 change in the exponent, and e^0.65 ≈ 1.9.
The chart's right side is drawn 250 million times taller than the left, and its energy axis is broken between 15 and 48 kJ/mol; the left side shows the crowd at 298 K (dashed) and now.
claims.source: Representation choice. Heights are f(E) = exp(-E/RT)/RT relative to f(0) at 298 K; right side multiplied by 2.5e8.

claims.text: 'About double per 10 K' is a rule of thumb that fits barriers near 50 kJ/mol around room temperature, not a law.
claims.source: From c3: the factor is exp[(Ea/R)(10/(T(T+10)))], so it depends on Ea and T; at 298 K it is 1.93 for 50 kJ/mol 1.48 for 30 kJ/mol and 2.50 for 70 kJ/mol (node script). Atkins & de Paula discuss the rule's limits.

recall.question: Why can a 10 K rise nearly double a reaction's rate when it is only about 3% hotter?
options: Every molecule moves twice as fast
The few collisions energetic enough to react nearly double
recall.why: Only the thin high-energy tail clears the barrier; a small warming barely moves the crowd but nearly doubles that tail.
